name: Privacy Regulation Theory
citation: Altman, I. (1975). The environment and social behavior. Brooks/Cole.

constructs.description: IC2 body-budget prediction + environmental predictability + IE-DPT activity frame configures interoceptive expectations.
Affordances + spatial enclosure + isovist control + environmental legibility enable boundary management.
Boundary violation + perceived control loss + interoceptive PE + allostatic demand. Density-is-not-crowding (Stokols) requires IE-DPT for explanation.
Social load deficit + DMN hyperengagement + dopaminergic deficit from lack of social stimulation.
Place recognition + hippocampal binding + learned safety signals establish spatial ownership.

irreducible_residual.narrative: The textbook IE-DPT bridge. Stokols' density-is-not-crowding finding is inexplicable without the explicit channel: the activity frame (IE-DPT) configures interoceptive expectations (IC), determining whether proximity generates positive or negative affective response. The open-plan office violates Privacy Regulation at multiple levels simultaneously.

key_references: Altman, I. (1975). The environment and social behavior. Brooks/Cole.
Stokols, D. (1972). On the distinction between density and crowding. Psychol. Rev., 79(3), 275-277.
Bernstein, E.S. & Turban, S. (2018). The impact of the open workspace. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 373(1753).

function_form.function_form: S(p) = |D(p) − A(p)|; D(p) = desired privacy level; A(p) = achieved level

variables.D(p): Desired privacy level (varies with activity, personality, culture)
variables.A(p): Achieved privacy level in current environment

predictions: Privacy deficit (D > A) produces crowding stress; excess (A > D) produces isolation
Open-plan offices: 50% of workers report privacy deficit as top complaint
